word:greek-nt:G0065.explanation: Agrielaios means a wild olive tree, or oleaster. Scripture contrasts this wild olive tree with a good olive tree when discussing grafting.

word:greek-nt:G0182.explanation: This word describes someone or something that lacks steadiness—restless, unsettled, or unstable rather than firm and consistent. It can describe an unsettled condition that does not remain constant. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in James: once rendered “unstable” and once “restless.” The surrounding verse determines how that lack of steadiness is expressed, but the central idea remains absence of stability.

word:greek-nt:G0326.explanation: Anazao means to come alive again or to revive.

word:greek-nt:G0379.explanation: This word describes someone as “inexcusable” or “without excuse”—a person who cannot rightly claim a defense for what has been done. It functions as an adjective, describing a condition of clear accountability rather than merely expressing disapproval. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Romans, where its meaning concerns the absence of a valid excuse. The precise force in each verse depends on its surrounding context.

word:greek-nt:G0454.explanation: Anoia means folly and can also describe madness.

word:greek-nt:G0595.explanation: Apothesis means putting off, laying down, or removal. It can describe putting away bodily filth or putting off a tent.

word:greek-nt:G0638.explanation: Apopnigō means to choke or suffocate. It can also describe drowning. When thorns choke what is growing with them, it describes stopping growth.

word:greek-nt:G0832.explanation: Auleō means to play the flute or pipe.

word:greek-nt:G0847.explanation: Autou means here. It can also mean there.

word:greek-nt:G0911.explanation: Baptō means to dip, as when a fingertip is dipped in water.

word:greek-nt:G1040.explanation: This word means “fine linen,” referring to high-quality linen cloth or garments made from it. It identifies a material rather than an action, person, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 16:19, so its normal meaning is established by this concise material description rather than by a broad range of uses. The precise significance of the linen in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its actual wording.

word:greek-nt:G1174.explanation: Deisidaimōn means religious or respectful toward what is divine.

word:greek-nt:G1206.explanation: This word means “on the following day” or “the next day.” It identifies the day immediately after a previously mentioned day, so its function is to mark the timing of an event or movement. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 28:13. Because it refers specifically to the next day, its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

word:greek-nt:G1259.explanation: This word means “be reconciled” or “to become reconciled.” It expresses the movement from estrangement or conflict toward restored peace between people. In a sentence, it refers to reconciliation rather than leaving a damaged relationship unresolved. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 5:24. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific force intended there.

word:greek-nt:G1343.explanation: Dikaiosynē means righteousness. It can also refer to divine righteousness. In one use, faith is counted as righteousness.

word:greek-nt:G1417.explanation: Dyo means two, marking a pair or number of two.

word:greek-nt:G1462.explanation: Enklēma means an accusation or charge.

word:greek-nt:G1545.explanation: Ekbasis means a way out or escape. It can also refer to the result or outcome of something.

word:greek-nt:G1624.explanation: Ektrepō means to turn aside or away. It can also mean to avoid something.

word:greek-nt:G1839.explanation: Exístēmi means to astonish or amaze. It can also describe being astonished. In another context, it refers to being beside oneself.

word:greek-nt:G1866.explanation: Epaenetus is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 16:5. The available wording preserves the name as “Epaenetus,” with “Epenetus” also representing it in English. Because this is a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of the person named, not a broader concept that can be defined like an ordinary noun or verb.

word:greek-nt:G1884.explanation: Eparkeō means to aid, help, or relieve.

word:greek-nt:G1963.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “thought.” It refers to mental content held in the mind—the inward thought itself. It functions as a noun, naming what a person is thinking rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 8:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the actual wording and surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a thought or inward mental consideration.

word:greek-nt:G2078.explanation: Eschatos means last. It can describe a final time, as in the last day.

word:greek-nt:G2171.explanation: Euche means a prayer or a vow.

word:greek-nt:G2214.explanation: Zētēsis means a question or inquiry. It can also describe a debate or controversy.

word:greek-nt:G2360.explanation: Throeo means to be troubled or alarmed.

word:greek-nt:G2485.explanation: Ichthudion means a small fish, or little fish.

word:greek-nt:G2522.explanation: Kathemerinos means daily, or day by day.

word:greek-nt:G2669.explanation: Kataponeō means to wear out or exhaust through labor or suffering. It can also mean to oppress.

word:greek-nt:G2715.explanation: Katexousiazō means to exercise authority over or rule over others. It is used of rulers exercising authority over people under them.

word:greek-nt:G2834.explanation: Cnidus is the name of a place. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs once, in Acts 27:7, and is rendered “Cnidus.” The word itself identifies the location rather than describing a person, action, quality, or spiritual condition. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is provided here, its broader significance must be understood from the travel narrative in which the name appears.

word:greek-nt:G2908.explanation: Kreitton means better, stronger, or more excellent, comparing one choice or condition with another.

word:greek-nt:G2997.explanation: Lakao means to burst open with a loud noise.

word:greek-nt:G3150.explanation: “Babble” or “meaningless talk” describes speech that lacks useful substance or purpose. It points to words that go on without producing understanding, truth, or a worthwhile result. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Timothy 1:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is speech that accomplishes nothing beneficial rather than communication with a useful purpose.

word:greek-nt:G3323.explanation: Messias means Messiah, the Anointed One.

word:greek-nt:G3428.explanation: Moichalis means an adulteress—a married woman who commits adultery. It can also refer figuratively to those who worship other than the true God.

word:greek-nt:G3525.explanation: Nēphō means to be sober. One passage contrasts being sober with sleeping and places it alongside watching.

word:greek-nt:G3590.explanation: Ogdoos means eighth. It can identify the eighth person among seven others.

word:greek-nt:G3631.explanation: Oinos means wine. It is presented as a drink and as the result of water being changed into it.

word:greek-nt:G3693.explanation: Opisthen means from behind. It can also mean after, as in bearing the cross after another person.

word:greek-nt:G3855.explanation: Paragō means to pass by or depart. It can also mean to pass away.

word:greek-nt:G3929.explanation: Paresis means overlooking or passing over; it can also refer to remission of sins that are past.

word:greek-nt:G3976.explanation: Pede means a shackle or fetter for the feet.

word:greek-nt:G4025.explanation: Perithesis means putting something around or on, as when wearing ornaments.

word:greek-nt:G4090.explanation: “Bitterly” describes an action done with bitterness or in a bitter manner. It is an adverb, so it tells how something is done rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice, and both occurrences are rendered “bitterly.” Its basic sense points to the intense, painful, or sorrowful quality accompanying an action, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force in each occurrence. The word appears in Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62.【p03:word:greek-nt:G4090:identity】【p03:word:greek-nt:G4090:occurrences】【p01:word:greek-nt:G4090:reference:0】【p01:word:greek-nt:G4090:reference:1】

word:greek-nt:G4128.explanation: Plethos means a multitude, crowd, or great number. It can describe many people gathered together, or a great number of fish.

word:greek-nt:G4227.explanation: Pudens is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing a quality, action, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, and its English rendering is simply “Pudens.” The available lexical information gives no additional definition beyond this name. Its occurrence is in 2 Timothy 4:21, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain what is said about the person there.

word:greek-nt:G4393.explanation: Prophero means to bring forth, produce, or bring out. In one use, it describes bringing good or evil out of the heart.

word:greek-nt:G4502.explanation: Rhoubēn is the personal name Reuben.

word:greek-nt:G4577.explanation: Seira means a chain or chains.

word:greek-nt:G4623.explanation: Siōpaō means to keep silent, be silent, or be quiet, whether by choice or not.

word:greek-nt:G4681.explanation: This word refers to Spain, a geographic region. It is a proper place-name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Romans 15, where Paul mentions Spain as part of his intended travel and ministry plans. The word itself identifies the destination; the surrounding passage is needed to understand Paul's fuller purpose in mentioning it.

word:greek-nt:G4744.explanation: Stilbō means to shine or glisten.

word:greek-nt:G4861.explanation: This word describes people who are harmonious and united in spirit. It expresses a shared inner outlook, emphasizing agreement and togetherness rather than merely being in the same place. In ordinary Bible reading, it points to people whose hearts and purposes move together. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Philippians 2:2; the surrounding verse context gives the particular force of the word there.

word:greek-nt:G4964.explanation: This word means “to conform to” or “to conform to a pattern.” It describes the action of shaping one’s conduct or character according to a pattern or model. As a verb, it expresses an active process of taking a form that corresponds to something else. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 12:2 and 1 Peter 1:14. Its exact force in either passage is clarified by the surrounding verse and its wider context.

word:greek-nt:G5000.explanation: Tabitha is a personal name for a Christian woman at Joppa.

word:greek-nt:G5347.explanation: Phēstos is the personal name Festus.

word:greek-nt:G5404.explanation: Φοίνικες means a palm tree or date-palm.

word:greek-nt:G5541.explanation: This word means “be kind”: to act with kindness toward others. It describes a person’s gracious, considerate way of treating people, rather than merely expressing a feeling of goodwill. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 13:4, so its normal meaning is represented by this single occurrence. The word functions as an action, describing what someone does in relation to others. Its precise force in that verse is understood more fully from the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G6016.explanation: διακαθᾶραι means to clear out or scour.

word:greek-nt:G6049.explanation: This word means “to stoop” or “to stoop down,” describing the physical act of bending the body forward or lowering oneself. It functions as an action word rather than a title or description of a person. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in John 8:8. The word itself identifies the movement, while the surrounding verse determines why the person stooped and what significance that action has in the scene.
